evidence.quote: Prerequisite(s): COMP 3511; Exclusion(s): COMP 5621, ELEC 3120, ISOM 3180;

sections.content: The course is not very difficult, and most of the topics are pretty basic. The slides cover the main ideas, but sometimes you may need to review a few parts by yourself. As long as you understand the important concepts, the course should be manageable.
sections.teaching: You do not really need to attend every lecture to do well in this course. Missing some classes is usually fine if you can study the material on your own. The lectures can still be useful for some topics.
sections.grading: There is a midterm and a final, and the exams are not too hard overall. However, you still need to spend some time studying before taking them. If you know the main concepts, getting a good grade should not be too difficult. I heard that some people barely studied and ended up failing, so it is better not to go in completely unprepared.
sections.workload: The workload is pretty light compared with many other courses. You do not need to spend a lot of time on it every week. Most of the work is just reviewing the material before the midterm and final. Studying for a few days before each exam should be enough for most people.

sections.content: Old, repetitive, and with some mistakes in the slides. The slides are not enough to fully understand the concepts. You can search for them or attend the class to fully understand them.
sections.teaching: I suggest attending the lectures as well. The instructor takes attendance sometimes (maybe two to three times in the whole semester). I'm not sure if they matter. 10% of each session is useful; the rest is not.
sections.grading: Not bad in grading. It's easy to get B+ and with a good understanding of the basics you can get an A.
sections.workload:
2 homeworks which were easy and 1 bonus homework which was easier.
No programming assignments.
The midterm and finals need some studying but they're also openbook (you can bring the slides to the exam).

sections.content: The content is not too much or too less. It does not cover web security but some other most common computer network basis. Application layer, transport layer, network layer, link layer and physic layer.
sections.teaching: The professor is very nice and gives a lot of examples to help students understand in class.
sections.grading: The grading is overall good. It seems everyone could achieve at least B, as long as no cheating.
sections.workload: There are 2 mandatory assignments to gain 30% scores. The third assignment is optional if you are happy with your first two assignments.

sections.teaching: I think it's good. The lessons are clear and interesting, and the content isn't difficult to understand.And even if you can't attend the lectures for some reason, reviewing the slides before the exam will be enough to help you easily learn most of the content.
sections.grading:
I believe that if you spend a normal amount of time preparing before the exam (or you master the basic content of the slides and assignments), it's difficult to get a score significantly lower than average. However, getting a high score isn't easy either.

Midterm exam is obviously more difficult than final exam. But getting a score above 80 on the final exam isn't always easy. This depends on luck and the grading criteria.
sections.workload:
There are three assignments in total, each with a relatively small number of questions, which is very manageable. Assignments account for 30% of the final grade. Only the two highest-scoring assignments are counted, meaning one assignment can be skipped. Overall, the workload on assignments is minimal.
If you never attend classes and haven't studied any related content, you can still prepare for the exam by reviewing your homework and slides before the exam, and the workload remains not heavy

sections.grading: If you want to spend some time on reviewing, you can get a good score at the final. BUT, more PhD students do not have time to review.
sections.workload: Two assignments. Its a very low workload. And the content of the course is very simple. BBB will teach much more less content even than a UG computer network course.

sections.content: The content is about the basic knowledge of network, even if you have never learnt about the network.

sections.grading: The grading is normal. I got the score above the average in the assignments, quiz and exams, and I got a B+.

sections.grading: The final exam was easy while the middle-term was difficult, but the final grade was acceptable.
sections.workload: Only three assignments without presentation or project. The assignments were very easy and it took about one hour to complete each.

sections.content: the content was quite interesting and easy to follow. it is okay not to know anything about networks and take this course, you will start with the very basics. The professor will ask in the beginning of the semester if you want to have more homework instead of a midterm. In my case, we had a midterm, a few small homeworks, and a final.
sections.teaching: The professor records all lectures and releases them for later review. His explanations are quite clear. If you have questions you better ask during the class. Questions on canvas were ignored lol.
sections.grading: The Midterm was very hard, but the final was easy. Since the homeworks and final were weighted more, he gave generous grading.
sections.workload: Questions covered in the homework and quizzes are not repeated in the exams. Homework is generally easy and does not take long to finish. There were 3 homework assignments on Canvas in total. The shark web exercises were optional and recommended for the exams. If you come to lectures you don't need to study extra to understand what's going on. Just look up for few example questions from the book to pass the quizzes.

sections.content: The course covered basic concepts of computer networking, which were quite similar to what I learned during my undergraduate studies. For students already familiar with networking fundamentals, the content was easy to grasp. However, it could have benefited from more advanced topics to challenge students further.
sections.teaching: The instructor's teaching was adequate, though I did not attend many sessions due to the introductory nature of the material. The lectures were clear but lacked the depth that would engage students more interested in exploring advanced aspects of networking.
sections.grading: The grading system was generally fair, but some of the questions were overly strict, especially when dealing with less common concepts. For example, missing a small detail like multiplying by two for the full-duplex and half-duplex concepts could result in significant point deductions. This felt a bit unreasonable, as it emphasized memorization over understanding.
sections.workload: The workload was light, mainly consisting of homework assignments and an exam. The assignments were not particularly difficult and didn’t require extensive effort, making it manageable for students balancing multiple courses. Overall, the course stress level was low.

sections.content: The content includes multiple aspects of networks, like Internet architecture， all kinds of protocols, and methods to facilitate large-scale networks, etc
sections.teaching: The professor exhibits exceptional prowess in teaching, making complex topics both accessible and engaging. His lectures are a blend of clarity and enthusiasm, where difficult concepts are broken down into understandable segments. He uses a variety of teaching methods, including interactive discussions, real-world examples, and thought-provoking questions, to stimulate deep thinking and foster a dynamic learning environment.
sections.grading: The grades were not particularly satisfying. I spent quite a lot of time reviewing the course materials, but the exam content turned out to be significantly more challenging than what was described in class. Although the majority of students are likely to receive a B+, the overall grading seems to be on the lower side, especially considering that the assignments were closely related to the course materials.
sections.workload: The workload for the course itself wasn't heavy, which is a cause for concern, as a significant portion of the exam content was not covered in the course materials. This necessitated gathering additional resources and studying on my own, thereby substantially increasing the workload outside of class.

sections.content: The course focuses on the architecture of the computer network, in a top-down perspective, including application layer, transport layer, network layer and link layer (physical layer is out of scope of the course).
sections.teaching: BENSAOU, Brahim taught very well, with fruitful examples to explain nearly each hard-to-understand concept in the course.
sections.grading: My grade is slightly higher than the mean score of the entire class. And my final GPA is B+. I think the score is OK for me.
sections.workload: The workload of the course is not high. We only have three homework assignments, a midterm exam and a final exam. Each homework assignment is easy and will not spend too much time.

Most of the students can get B+. I was a bit below mean in both midterm and final but I still received B+ as final grade.

btw. A previous comment says that prof will not give B+ to non-phd student. This is not true. I am a non-phd student and I have asked professor about this. He said the grade was only based on your homework and exam results.

Both midterm and final are open book. The note can only be taken from the powerpoint or in-class note.
